title: The crossing lost the beat
subtitle: How a real edit got back on the piano, and what a replay still missed.
request: Keep the song’s ownership story moving. Give the singer visible performance, fit the lettering into the world, and land the piano crossings on the beat.
evidenceAtTheTime: The original film, the lyric cut, the exact stereo master and the retained takes were already on hand. The opening used deliberate voice-over. Sung passages and instrumental gaps needed different coverage.
historicalAttempt: The in-scene cut put lettering on several surfaces while retiming crossings and adding visible chorus performance.
ownerFeedback: The artist preferred the earlier edit, rejected the lettering and kept the lip-sync. That response preserved a specific part of an otherwise rejected attempt.
actualCorrection: The earlier picture became the base. The accepted vocal inserts and original stereo track stayed. The unwanted lettering was removed, and later rhythm inserts and a keyboard cutaway were repaired.
actualResult: The artist approved the Rhythm Cut on 26 November 2026. The published film preserves the accepted performance.

comparison.question: Could a more explicit prompt help a model plan the next cut from the evidence available at the time?

arms.name: Current guidance
arms.excerpt: syncs piano key crossings to the beat
arms.observation: Named the right rhythmic action. It still omitted separate handling of voice-over and a small unlettered comparison.

arms.name: Revised prompt
arms.observation: The action conflicted with the request and with its own verification line.

arms.name: Revised prompt with retrieved example
arms.observation: Reached the shared response token cap without returning proposal text.

comparison.conclusion: The revised prompt covered fewer requirements on this pilot. The retrieval proposal was unavailable for quality review. Keep the current guidance and test a narrower revision on fresh cases.

evidenceViews.name: Intelligence
evidenceViews.example: The revised action put the piano crossing off-beat despite a correct-sounding verification line.

evidenceViews.name: Wisdom
evidenceViews.scope: Small lettering sample with an unlettered comparison
evidenceViews.example: Both proposals put lettering into the preview without isolating the risk to a single inspectable sample.

evidenceViews.name: Endurance
evidenceViews.scope: Proposals returned under the response limit
evidenceViews.example: Two arms filled both cases. The third reached its cap without an answer.

evidenceViews.name: Creativity
evidenceViews.scope: An external mechanism and meaningful portfolio alternatives
evidenceViews.example: Both suggested broad neon prototype passes without the alternative compositions required for a comparison.

evidenceViews.name: Knowledge
evidenceViews.scope: Prior edit and exact stereo clock preserved in the proposal
evidenceViews.example: Both kept the source edit and recording in their proposed next pass.

evidenceViews.name: Alignment
evidenceViews.scope: Beat, vocal mode and owner criticism handled
evidenceViews.example: The revised prompt mishandled the beat and proposed keeping two portfolio lead images the owner had questioned.

evidenceViews.name: Craft
evidenceViews.observation: The artist accepted the Rhythm Cut after rejecting the in-scene typography treatment and keeping the performances.

evidenceViews.name: Impact
evidenceViews.scope: Audience or adoption outcomes attributable to the replay

methodLimit: Two grouped cases and one proposal pass per variant. The reviewer used a frozen rubric and shuffled response labels, and had seen prompt lengths during setup. Only the historical edit received owner acceptance. The replay tested planning proposals without tools, media analysis or deployment.
